A1.notes.Q3: As an advisor, grades feel relevant, but high school data feels invasive and irrelevant to current university struggles. Activity logs on Absalon are borderline; useful for early signals if the gain is clear.
A1.notes.Q4: I cannot explain a 'black box' to a distressed student or defend the university's decision. We need clear reasons to build trust and offer tailored help, so I will not accept very low explainability.
A1.notes.Q5: Missing vulnerable students is worse than contacting a few who don't need it yet. However, we must ensure the model doesn't systematically ignore specific groups like first-generation students.
A1.notes.Q6: Mass emails are ignored; personal invitations are effective but resource-heavy. A balanced approach with two check-ins per year allows timely support without overwhelming staff or students.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's safe to cast a wide net. For personalized outreach from an advisor, we need better precision to respect their time and avoid unnecessary anxiety.
A1.Q8.1: We must ensure that 'support' isn't just surveillance. Students need to know they can opt out of this specific predictive tracking without penalty to their standard studies.

A2.notes.Q3: As an advisor, I see clear value in academic performance data. However, login logs feel like surveillance. Sensitive data is a red line unless it specifically fixes bias against vulnerable groups.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is our currency with students. If I cannot explain why a student was flagged, I cannot effectively support them. A 'black box' breaks the advisor-student relationship.
A2.notes.Q5: We must not miss struggling students due to bias. Missing a vulnerable student is worse than contacting a few who are fine. I'm willing to trade slight overall accuracy for equal opportunity.
A2.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored; personalized notes show care. Waiting until the end of the year is too late. Intervention must be immediate when signs appear, but always voluntary.
A2.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's better to over-include than miss someone in crisis. For personalized contact, we must be more careful to protect student dignity and avoid alarm fatigue.
A2.Q8.1: We need clear guidelines on who sees the data. Students must know they can opt out of being flagged without penalty to their academic standing or relationship with advisors.

A3.notes.Q3: As an advisor, I see how hard it is to reach students before they drop out. Course grades help predict struggles well, but tracking login activity feels like surveillance unless the gain is huge. Sensitive data should only be used to fix bias or if it's crucial for identifying at-risk groups.
A3.notes.Q4: I need to explain to students why they are contacted to build trust. A black box model makes me uncomfortable as I have to advocate for the system. Even a slight gain isn't worth losing the ability to say 'the model saw X' clearly.
A3.notes.Q5: Missing students in marginalized groups is unacceptable; it deepens inequality. I am willing to accept fewer total correct identifications if it means we don't systematically overlook vulnerable students. Our duty of care requires us to catch everyone who needs help, not just the easy-to-predict ones.
A3.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored; students need to feel seen and supported personally. A personalized note from an advisor followed by a voluntary meeting works best. Continuous monitoring is better than yearly checks, as struggles can happen at any time in the semester.
A3.notes.Q7: For general info, it's safer to contact slightly more students; a non-urgent email is low cost. For personalized outreach, we must be careful not to alarm those who don't need help. The threshold should balance reaching the vulnerable with respecting privacy.
A3.Q8.1: We must ensure that 'support' doesn't become a path to forced study plans or disciplinary action. Students need to know this is strictly for offering help, not gathering evidence against them.

S1.notes.Q3: I was a dropout, so grades matter early on. But tracking my Absalon clicks feels like surveillance. First-gen status helps me get support without needing to beg for it.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to trust the university. If they just say 'a computer said so', I'll feel judged and ignored, not helped.
S1.notes.Q5: We shouldn't miss anyone who needs help. It's worse to leave a struggling student behind than to accidentally email one person who is doing fine.
S1.notes.Q6: A generic email feels less scary than a phone call from a stranger I don't know, but I'd definitely go to an advisor if invited voluntarily.
S1.notes.Q7: If it's just info, send it to many. If it's a personalized message implying I'm failing, only contact me if the risk is really high.
S1.Q8.1: Make sure students can opt out or correct data errors easily. As a re-starter, my past failure shouldn't define my current potential forever.

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student working part-time, my 'Absalon' data is poor because I focus on work hours, not clicks. Tracking logs misinterprets hardworking students as struggling. Sensitive data like nationality or race must never be used; first-gen status helps understand specific barriers.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged, especially if the model assumes international students struggle more due to my background. If a 'black box' says I'm at risk without clear reasons like low credits or failed exams, I will distrust it and ignore support.
S2.notes.Q5: It is unfair if the model misses students from non-EU backgrounds because they learn differently. We need equal recall so no group is overlooked due to data bias. I prefer missing fewer at-risk students over reducing false alarms.
S2.notes.Q6: A direct phone call feels too intrusive and aggressive for a student working full-time to survive. A personalized email is okay, but a voluntary meeting invitation is best—it respects my time while offering real help immediately.
S2.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's better to contact many; ignoring someone in trouble is worse than a slight annoyance. For personalized messages from an advisor, we must be more careful and balanced to respect the student's dignity.
S2.Q8.1: The university must explicitly acknowledge that non-EU students often work more hours and have less time for 'Absalon' tracking or social integration. Models trained on local data might flag us as struggling when we are just managing dual responsibilities.

S3.notes.Q3: As someone with a chronic condition, I fear data about my disability being used against me or creating bias. Grades are fine for context, but tracking daily activity feels like surveillance.
S3.notes.Q4: If the system flags me, I need to know why to trust it and fix my situation. A black box is terrifying; if you can't explain the risk, I won't believe the help.
S3.notes.Q5: It is better to reach fewer students overall than to miss those who already struggle due to background or disability. We must ensure marginalized groups are not left behind.
S3.notes.Q6: A generic email is too easy to ignore when you are overwhelmed. A personalized message or a voluntary meeting feels supportive, not punitive. Support should be available immediately.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's better to err on the side of caution and reach out too much. For personalized contacts involving an advisor, we must be more precise to respect time and privacy.
S3.Q8.1: The model should never use my disability data to predict failure, as this assumes I will fail because of my condition rather than recognizing my potential with support.

S4.notes.Q3: As someone with ADHD, I know my struggles aren't just about grades. Absalon data helps see procrastination, but sensitive data feels like surveillance unless it fixes bias against students like me.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know *why* I was flagged. If it's a black box, I can't address the root cause of my difficulties or trust the advice.
S4.notes.Q5: I don't want to be missed because the model was trained on 'typical' students. It is better to catch fewer people overall than to miss those with neurodivergent or non-traditional paths.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored; personalized ones feel caring, not spying. Contacting me twice a year fits my rhythm without overwhelming my anxiety.
S4.notes.Q7: For generic info, cast a wide net to catch everyone who might need it. For personalized contact, be careful; false positives can feel like a label I can't escape.
S4.Q8.1: The model must not use my data to punish me later (e.g., in admissions or recommendations). I also need an easy way to opt-out of being flagged entirely if I'm coping fine despite 'risk' signals.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, I worry that data like nationality or high-school background could bias the system against me before I even start. Using grades is okay if it helps, but tracking my every click on Absalon feels invasive.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged, especially with different teaching styles here. If the reason is hidden, I feel targeted rather than supported. A 'black box' system destroys trust immediately.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; if the model misses international students because it was trained on local data, those of us struggling most get no help. Better to contact fewer people overall than to systematically exclude specific groups.
S5.notes.Q6: Unsolicited phone calls are too aggressive for a first year student new to the system. A gentle, personalized email offering resources feels safer and respects my autonomy while still signaling support.
S5.notes.Q7: For generic emails, I prefer a balance to avoid spam. But for personalized outreach, it is better to err on the side of contacting more students, as missing someone in crisis is worse than an unnecessary check-in.
S5.Q8.1: The university must ensure that any model is regularly audited for bias against non-EU students, as our educational backgrounds differ significantly from the Danish norm used for training data.

S6.notes.Q3: Using grades is okay if it helps slightly, but never admit sensitive data like nationality or background. As an EU student who dropped out before, I fear profiling based on my history.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to trust the system. A 'black box' model feels like surveillance, not support. If it's too complex to explain, don't use it.
S6.notes.Q5: We must catch students who might otherwise fall through the cracks due to bias. It is better to miss a few if it means we stop missing people from marginalized groups.
S6.notes.Q6: A generic email feels cold and robotic. I'd prefer a personal note or a voluntary meeting. Checking in twice a year seems enough without being harassing.
S6.notes.Q7: If it's just an email, cast a wider net. But if the message is personalized and sensitive, accuracy must be higher to avoid embarrassment or mistrust.
S6.Q8.1: The language barrier aspect is crucial for international students like me. Models trained on Danish context might misinterpret my academic behavior as 'difficulty' when it's just adaptation issues.

S7.notes.Q3: As a student with dyslexia, my academic struggles often aren't visible in grades initially. While course performance helps, using admission data feels like judging me by my past rather than current potential. However, knowing I need extra time could genuinely help target support if the gain is significant.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged. If a black box says 'you are struggling,' it feels dismissive, especially when my dyslexia means standard metrics don't tell the full story. A clear explanation allows me to address specific issues rather than feeling stigmatized.
S7.notes.Q5: It is worse to miss students like me who need help because the system doesn't understand our learning differences, even if it flags a few others unnecessarily. Missing support can lead to dropout; unnecessary contact is just annoying.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easily ignored or deleted. A personalized message acknowledging my situation and a voluntary meeting feels safer and more useful than a generic alert. As soon as I start falling behind, I need help, not a yearly check-in.
S7.notes.Q7: For general info, slightly many is okay. But for personalized support that actually helps students with disabilities succeed, we should cast a wider net. It is better to invite someone who doesn't need it than to miss the person who desperately does.
S7.Q8.1: The biggest fear is that such models will reinforce biases against students with learning difficulties if the training data reflects past failures without context. We must ensure the model understands that lower grades might reflect a disability accommodation issue, not lack of ability or effort.

S8.notes.Q3: I need improvement to accept tracking my login habits or grades beyond credits. I fear profiling based on origin, but knowing first-gen status could help target support for students like me who struggled before.
S8.notes.Q4: If the system flags me, I must understand why to trust it. A 'black box' feels like a trap. High explainability is essential for building a genuine relationship with an advisor.
S8.notes.Q5: I don't want to be missed because I come from the Faroe Islands. It's better to contact more students generally if it ensures no one from a minority group is overlooked in silence.
S8.notes.Q6: A generic email is good first contact; a forced call feels intrusive. I'd prefer checking in twice a year rather than constantly, which might feel like surveillance.
S8.notes.Q7: With general info, it's okay to reach out to more people; they can just ignore it. But personalized messages should be balanced carefully so we don't feel judged or misunderstood.
S8.Q8.1: As a student who dropped out once before, I worry that being labeled 'at risk' too early could become a self-fulfilling prophecy if the support feels like punishment rather than genuine help.

S9.notes.Q3: As a non-EU student with a disability, I fear bias from nationality or socioeconomic data. However, tracking my learning activity could genuinely help if it flags invisible struggles caused by my condition.
S9.notes.Q4: If I am flagged, I must know why to trust the advice. Black boxes feel like surveillance. A 'black box' decision is too risky for my mental health and privacy.
S9.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is worse than contacting a few unnecessarily. Students like me, with hidden disabilities, are often overlooked by standard metrics, so we must prioritize catching everyone.
S9.notes.Q6: No phone calls; that feels too intrusive. An email first gives me space to prepare, followed by a voluntary meeting if I choose. Twice a year fits my thesis pace.
S9.notes.Q7: With generic info, it's safer to cast a wide net. Personalized messages carry more weight and risk of stigma if wrong, so they need stricter accuracy.
S9.Q8.1: Crucial missing point: Who trains the model? If data comes from successful students without disabilities or foreign backgrounds, it will inherently fail us who struggle differently.
